headline: US strikes Iran near the Strait of Hormuz, oil jumps 3.5%, while PLS and GXAI lead today's ASX portfolio losses.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara dropped 3.24% today in a rough session for lithium stocks. No fresh company-specific news drove the move — it's continued weakness in the lithium price outlook. PLS is down 33.5% on your cost base, a reflection of how far lithium has fallen from its 2022 peak. The long-term EV thematic is still intact, but this is a story that needs patience.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: The AI ETF fell 3.03% today. No major fund-specific news — the main item was an administrative change: Global X Australia relocated its registered office to 20 Martin Place, Sydney, affecting 47 ETFs including this one. That's purely housekeeping with no impact on the fund itself. The dip looks like broader market nerves around geopolitical risk (US-Iran tensions) rather than anything structural with AI.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two slipped 1.18% last night. No specific news came out — it looks like general risk-off selling as investors got cautious ahead of the US-Iran escalation. The GTA VI story hasn't changed; this is just short-term noise for a long-term hold.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: Google edged down a tiny 0.34% last night — essentially flat. News flow was positive: reports highlight Google leaning on AI growth and ad resilience as key pillars. A minimal dip with no negative catalyst — the long-term story looks fine.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG slipped a modest 0.20% today — barely worth noting. As a diversified multi-asset fund, this is just daily noise. The ASX 200 was virtually flat today, which explains the small move.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS edged up 0.24% today, reflecting last night's positive Wall Street session where the S&P 500 gained 0.42%. A steady, quiet day for this broad US market exposure.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft rose 0.19% last night and is being flagged as one of the 'safest earnings plays' by retail investors, according to Stocktwits chatter, even amid US-Iran geopolitical jitters. Citi analysts also named MSFT among their top three tech buys ahead of earnings. Sitting at a $52.86 AUD unrealised loss on your position, but the near-term sentiment is improving.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE was the standout today, gaining 0.53%. Emerging market sentiment got a small lift from positive economic signals — the IMF raised Brazil's 2026 growth forecast to 2.4%, and there's broader talk of emerging markets benefiting from global economic recovery. A nice quiet winner today.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX — sitting 33% in the red, but hold your nerve
watch_today.detail: Pilbara dropped another 3.24% today and is your biggest drag at -$50.30 AUD. The lithium market remains soft with no near-term price catalyst visible. However, for a long-term holder the EV battery thematic is still very much alive — lithium demand is a structural story that plays out over years, not months. Nothing has broken the investment thesis. Sit tight.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX — AI ETF down 3%, but long-term AI story intact
watch_today.detail: GXAI dropped 3.03% today and is now -13.64% on your cost base (-$40.52 AUD). Today's fall looks more like geopolitical risk-off selling than any problem with AI as a sector. The administrative office move for Global X is meaningless to fund performance. For a long-term AI believer, this is noise — hold.

watch_today.title: Oil spiked 3.5% on US strikes against Iran — watch the ripple effects
watch_today.detail: The US launched a new wave of strikes against Iran near the Strait of Hormuz overnight, sending crude oil (WTI) up 3.5% to $73.91/barrel. The Strait of Hormuz is the world's most critical oil shipping lane — any disruption there moves energy prices fast. Higher oil means higher fuel costs for businesses and consumers, which can feed back into inflation. Watch whether this escalates further this week.

watch_today.title: MSFT earnings approaching — Citi likes it as a buy
watch_today.detail: Microsoft ticked up 0.19% last night and is getting analyst love ahead of upcoming earnings, with Citi naming it one of their top three tech buys. Retail sentiment is also warming, calling it the 'safest earnings play' despite geopolitical noise. You're currently -$52.86 AUD on this position — earnings could be a turning point. Hold and watch.

watch_today.title: Westpac flags possible RBA rate hike — bad for growth stocks
watch_today.detail: Westpac has signalled it believes the RBA (Reserve Bank of Australia) may hike interest rates again. Rate hikes are bad news for growth-oriented assets like GXAI and VTS because they make future earnings worth less in today's money. Keep an eye on any RBA commentary this week — it could weigh on your ASX growth holdings.

watch_today.title: TTWO — hold steady, no new negative news
watch_today.detail: Take-Two fell 1.18% last night but there's no company-specific bad news. This looks like broader market caution on US-Iran tensions. You're up 6% on this position overall — the GTA VI cycle thesis remains intact. No reason to act.

world.summary: The dominant story today is the escalating US-Iran conflict, with fresh American strikes near the Strait of Hormuz pushing oil prices sharply higher. Separately, Trump is moving aggressively to reshape US election rules ahead of the midterms, and China's digital currency is quietly gaining ground as a global trade settlement tool.

stories.title: US launches new wave of strikes against Iran near the Strait of Hormuz
stories.why_it_matters: The US has carried out a fresh round of military strikes against Iran, targeting sites near the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway through which roughly 20% of the world's oil flows. Iran responded by declaring that diplomacy has proven 'futile', signalling a hardening position. The immediate market impact was crude oil jumping 3.5% to $73.91 a barrel. If the Strait were disrupted even briefly, global energy prices would spike sharply, hitting petrol prices and inflation worldwide — including here in Australia.

stories.title: Trump moves to tighten federal control of US elections ahead of midterms
stories.why_it_matters: President Trump is pushing through a series of moves to centralise federal control over how US elections are run, ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. Critics — including The Guardian and SBS — describe it as 'an all-out assault' on the independence of the US electoral system. Traditionally, US elections are run at the state level; shifting control to the federal government could alter who gets to vote, how ballots are counted, and which races are competitive. This is shaping up as one of the biggest domestic political battles in the US this year.

stories.title: Iran bets Trump will blink first as nuclear talks stall
stories.why_it_matters: Even as the US launches military strikes, Iran appears to be playing a strategic waiting game — betting that domestic pressure on Trump (high oil prices, economic costs) will force the US back to the negotiating table before Iran has to make concessions. The AFR reports Tehran is counting on Trump's unpredictability working in their favour. This diplomatic deadlock is the backdrop to rising oil prices and means the conflict could drag on without a clear resolution, keeping energy markets on edge.

stories.title: Australia toughens travel warnings for UAE and Qatar — even for transit passengers
stories.why_it_matters: Australia's Smartraveller service has toughened its travel advice for the UAE and Qatar, now explicitly stating that 'transit is travel' — meaning even if you're just changing planes in Dubai or Doha, the elevated risk warnings apply to you. This is directly linked to the US-Iran military escalation, with Gulf states potentially caught in the crossfire of any wider regional conflict. If you have flights booked through those hubs, it's worth checking your travel insurance and the latest government advice.

stories.title: China's digital yuan quietly becoming a global trade settlement tool
stories.why_it_matters: China's digital yuan (e-CNY) is increasingly being used to settle international trade deals, particularly with countries looking to reduce reliance on the US dollar — a strategy called 'monetary hedging'. As US-Iran tensions rise and more countries seek alternatives to dollar-based transactions, China's digital currency could gain meaningful traction. For Australian investors, this is a slow-burn story: if the US dollar's dominance in global trade erodes even slightly, it shifts the geopolitical and financial landscape in ways that affect everything from commodity prices to exchange rates.

politics.summary: Two key domestic stories today: Westpac is flagging the possibility of another RBA interest rate rise, and Labor is caught in an internal dispute over whether AI companies should be allowed to train on copyright-protected creative work without paying for it.

stories.title: Westpac signals another RBA interest rate hike could be coming
stories.why_it_matters: Westpac — one of Australia's Big Four banks — has put out a signal that the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) may lift the official cash rate again. A rate hike would mean higher mortgage repayments for millions of Australians and generally cools spending in the economy. For investors, it's bad news for growth-focused assets (higher rates make future profits worth less today) and could weigh on property prices. With inflation still sticky, the RBA is clearly not done yet in Westpac's view.

stories.title: Labor internally split over AI companies using creative works without permission
stories.why_it_matters: AI companies — including international tech giants — are lobbying the Australian government to weaken copyright law so they can legally use writers', musicians', and artists' creative work to train AI models without paying for it. Australia's creative industries are furious, saying this would let billion-dollar companies steal their livelihoods. Labor is internally divided on the issue, with some MPs sympathetic to the tech industry's argument that tight copyright rules will stifle AI development in Australia. The outcome will set a precedent for how AI is built and who gets paid in Australia going forward.

ai.summary: AI governance and regulation is the dominant theme today — from protests outside OpenAI's offices to Elon Musk calling for a new US regulatory body, and Meta quietly launching a new AI model for developers.

stories.title: Hundreds protest outside OpenAI and Anthropic offices in San Francisco
stories.why_it_matters: Hundreds of protesters gathered outside the San Francisco offices of OpenAI (maker of ChatGPT) and Anthropic (maker of Claude) over the weekend. The protests reflect growing public anger about AI development moving too fast without enough safety guardrails or accountability. It's a sign that AI companies are facing real political and social pressure — not just regulatory pressure — which could eventually force them to slow down or change how they operate.

stories.title: Elon Musk calls for an independent AI regulatory agency in the US
stories.why_it_matters: Elon Musk has publicly called for the creation of an independent AI regulatory agency in the United States — essentially an equivalent of the FDA (food and drug regulator) but for artificial intelligence. This is a notable flip from Musk's earlier anti-regulation stance. Given his ownership of xAI (maker of Grok) and his political connections to the Trump administration, this call carries real weight. If the US creates such an agency, it would reshape how AI products are approved and deployed globally, including products used in Australia.

stories.title: Meta launches Muse Spark 1.1 AI model for developers
stories.why_it_matters: Meta (owner of Facebook and Instagram) has quietly launched Muse Spark 1.1, a new AI model being made available through a developer API — meaning software developers can now plug Meta's AI directly into their own apps and products. This is Meta's move to compete with OpenAI and Google in the 'AI infrastructure' market, where companies pay to use AI brains in their own products. More competition in this space is generally good for users (lower prices, more options) but puts pressure on all the big players including Google (which you hold via GOOG).

stories.title: Mark Zuckerberg returns to X (formerly Twitter) for the first time in three years
stories.why_it_matters: Mark Zuckerberg made his first appearance on X (the platform formerly known as Twitter, bought by Elon Musk for $44 billion) after a three-year absence. The two have been fierce public rivals — they even briefly discussed a cage fight. Zuckerberg's return to X is being read as a signal that the rivalry may be thawing, or at minimum that he sees value in the platform's reach. In the AI world, Musk (xAI/Grok) and Zuckerberg (Meta AI) are direct competitors — any shift in their relationship is worth watching.

stories.title: AI regulation diverges sharply across Europe, UK, and US financial sectors
stories.why_it_matters: A new analysis shows that Europe, the UK, and the US are each taking very different approaches to regulating AI in financial services. Europe is going with strict rules and compliance requirements; the UK is taking a lighter, principles-based approach; and the US remains largely hands-off. For Australian investors in global tech stocks, this fragmented regulatory landscape means companies like Google and Microsoft face different rulebooks in each major market — adding compliance costs and risk in some regions while enjoying freedom in others.

sport.summary: The NRL Round 19 wrap is in, with Melbourne Storm saving their season in a thriller against the Titans, and Wayne Bennett's tactical masterstroke leading a Broncos win over the Knights. Cruz Hewitt grabbed Wimbledon headlines but came up short in the Boys' Final. Round 20 kicks off Thursday.

stories.title: Storm save their season in a last-gasp thriller against the Titans
stories.why_it_matters: Melbourne Storm pulled off a dramatic last-minute win over the Gold Coast Titans to keep their season alive. It's a massive result for Storm's finals hopes and a gutting loss for the Titans, who were brave but couldn't hold on. For Gold Coast fans, the Titans play Sea Eagles at Cbus Super Stadium this Sunday in Round 20 — another must-watch local game.

stories.title: Wayne Bennett's masterstroke as Knights' wild comeback falls short — Broncos win
stories.why_it_matters: Wayne Bennett pulled off a tactical masterstroke to guide the Broncos past the Knights, despite a wild comeback attempt from Newcastle that nearly got over the line. The article refers to a birthday celebration for Jai Arrow, adding a colourful backdrop to the Broncos' win. The Broncos face the Panthers at CommBank Stadium this Thursday night to open Round 20 — a top-of-the-table feel to that one.

stories.title: Cruz Hewitt loses Wimbledon Boys' Final but sets sights on Australian Open
stories.why_it_matters: Cruz Hewitt — son of Lleyton Hewitt — lost the Wimbledon Boys' Singles Final in heartbreaking fashion, but said he has no regrets: 'That little kid would be happy.' At 18, he's transitioning from junior to senior tennis and has declared his major goal is now to qualify for and compete at the Australian Open. He told reporters he's 'trending in the right direction' after making the final of the world's most prestigious grass-court event. A genuine Australian talent to follow.

stories.title: Gorden Tallis drops $700,000 truth bomb on Parramatta Eels over Jarome Luai deal
stories.why_it_matters: NRL legend Gorden Tallis has publicly questioned Parramatta Eels' $700,000 deal to sign halfback Jarome Luai, calling it a massive financial risk for a club that's been struggling. Luai is currently the subject of rumours about an alleged falling-out with Tigers coach Benji Marshall — separate Instagram activity from both camps has fuelled speculation. The Eels are on a bye in Round 20, giving the club a week to let the off-field noise die down before Luai is expected to join.

stories.title: GWS Giants topple Geelong Cats in AFL thriller despite injuries everywhere
stories.why_it_matters: The GWS Giants overcame a massive deficit and injuries across their lineup to beat the Geelong Cats in a stunning comeback. It continued the Cats' troubling recent form — with a separate AFL analyst report titled 'There are problems everywhere' for Geelong, flagging major concerns about their season falling apart. The Giants win keeps them firmly in the finals picture heading into the back half of the AFL season.

markets.summary: The ASX barely moved today, closing almost flat at 8,808. The big news from last night's US session was a 3.5% spike in oil prices after the US struck Iran near the Strait of Hormuz. Wall Street managed to stay positive despite the geopolitical shock, with the S&P 500 up 0.42% and the Nasdaq up 0.29%. Gold pulled back slightly. The Aussie dollar is essentially unchanged at 69.35 US cents.

indicators.note: Flat session — the ASX barely budged today despite the oil spike and geopolitical tension overnight.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's session: Wall Street held firm despite US-Iran tensions, with the S&P 500 gaining 0.42%.

indicators.name: NASDAQ
indicators.note: Last night's session: Tech stocks edged higher, driven by AI optimism and positive Microsoft sentiment ahead of earnings.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: The big mover last night — oil jumped 3.5% after US strikes against Iran near the Strait of Hormuz, the world's key oil shipping lane.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold pulled back 0.87% despite rising geopolitical risk — unusual, but may reflect profit-taking after recent highs above $4,100.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar is barely changed, down just 0.14% to 69.35 US cents. Steady as she goes.
